 History written as ICC's smallest member wins home T20I series
 Falkland Islands public flock to ground in Stanley to watch team beat Costa Rica.
 20 November, 2026 Picture courtesy of Falkland Islands Cricket Association 
 By Daniel Beswick 
 The first chapters of international cricket held by the ICC's smallest member have been written this week, off the mainland of South America.
 The Falkland Islands made the Platinum Ground in the capital of Stanley a fortress in their men's T20I series against Costa Rica , claiming a 6-2 win.
 And it was not just a first for cricket on the Falklands - it's considered the first international sporting action ever hosted on the islands that is recognised by its international governing body.
 Photo credit: Falkland Islands Cricket 
 There is just one commercial flight a week to the Falklands, running to and from Santiago in Chile, and the territory’s tourist board has a “Getting Here” tab on its website as a need of clarity for the curious traveller. Those on Antarctic expeditions sometimes stop by on the islands, though visitors largely consist of those on military assignment.
 To give you an idea of how small the Falklands are in terms of people, you can fit its entire population of around 3,800 people into the Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad and still have about 128,000 vacant seats. In terms of ICC Members, even Saint Helena, the next-smallest ICC Member by population, has them covered by at least a thousand people.
 Platinum Oval in the town of Stanley is further south than New Zealand’s international grounds in Dunedin and Queenstown, and just over a 1000 kilometres from Antarctic land.
 Players walk off in Stanley during the Falkland Islands/Costa Rica T20I series. Photo: Falklands TV 
 With all these factors considered, it means a small window for any cricket at all, let alone an international series and accommodating for overseas guests.
 Despite the hurdles, it hasn't stopped a cricketing nation wanting to make a splash in the game.
 “For us to plan anything, we need a year plus or almost, and not just flights,” Falkland Islands captain, coach and secretary Cecil Alexander tells ICC Digital from the ground’s clubhouse after play in their bilateral series with Costa Rica.
 “People have to take leave. You need to get the finances in order. And, Costa Rica was willing to work with us, holding this bilateral series.” 
 “Working around something that's only once a week (a flight in and out of the country) makes it difficult.
 The teams were able to squeeze eight matches into their tight window, even after a shift in scheduling mid-series to accomodate for inclement weather and conditions.
 “The weather is not ideal. Sometimes it can be quite windy and not that warm. So it's very challenging to even consider hosting something like this because a lot of things can go wrong," Alexander added.
 “From late October, sometimes early November and then into March, if we're lucky, we can go into April with regards to outdoor matches. After that, the temperature goes well below zero sometimes, and obviously (with) snow. It gets just under zero degrees, during the winter with a couple of snowfalls. And then in the summer, if we are lucky, it gets 19, 20 degrees.
 “So the past few days, I think the temperature was 11 or 12 degrees, with about 13, 14 mile-an-hour winds, which we here would actually consider a fairly pleasant day under normal circumstances.”
 Despite the barren conditions and the island's position, history of cricket in the Falklands goes back to at least the 1920s and 1930s, with early organised matches played by a local team representing Stanley against players from visiting ships and military. Matches in the 1960s and 1970s were played between Stanley Cricket Club and the local Dependencies Survey (the predecessor of the British Antarctic Survey) and those from naval ships.
 After a dip in popularity, the game found impetus in the late 1980s and 1990s, and after forming the Falkland Islands Cricket Association in 2001, sponsorship and fundraising powered cricket on the islands in a successful push to become an ICC Member in 2007. They along other Affiliates became Associate members in 2017 after the governing body’s move to a two-tier system.
 Nine years on, the Falklands men ensured their crowning moment would not be scuppered by the visitors, beating them twice on the first day of the series, chasing down 112 and 144 with ease in front of what felt like the entire town in the eyes of Alexander on a long weekend Monday for King Charles III's birthday.
 “There were a lot of people, on the top deck, in the clubhouse and around, and it was just really wonderful to have a good crowd behind us on the sides. Also just cheering for every catch, cheering for every run saved," he added.
 "It was really good that the community was quite involved and very supportive. 
 “There's a lot of other activities that also happened over the weekend, so there was a lot going on, but we had a really good turnout for the cricket as well.
 “And I definitely think we've made some believers out of that, that Cricket is an interesting sport to watch.”
 The series may well have given the youngsters on the boundaries some heroes to look up to as well if performances during the series are to go by.
 Phillip Stroud showed his all-round qualities in the eight matches, and has a rare double of representing the two-smallest ICC Members in international cricket, having also represented Saint Helena in African action, albeit before the universal awarding of T20I status in 2018.
 After moving to the Falklands, Cricket has also taken him to Bermuda, where he was selected in an ICC Americas Select tour, bringing together players across the region to further develop their game. Stroud made the first half-century in an official T20I for the Falklands in Costa Rica in 2025, with Alexander a man of his word after vowing before the series to shave his head if any player raised their bat.
 Cecil put down the same challenge in the home series, and lost out again thanks to his brother Jaco Alexander. Jaco thundered with the bat in the series, making 376 runs at average of over 75, with Eric Gildenhuys' nine wickets coming at 16.66.
 Jaco leads the team for runs and wickets in official T20Is (the side also played matches away against Costa Rica with official status in 2026) and moved to the islands nine years ago, with Cecil following months later.
 Cecil meanwhile is commended for his bowling, and not just on the cricket field, having also competed at recent Commonwealth Games in lawn bowls. He defeated Kenya’s Anwar Hamada in singles play, and also pushed former outdoor World Champion Ryan Bester to a tie break.
 Cecil Alexander wears many hats in the Falklands sporting community. Photo: Falkland Islands Cricket Association 
 Though for an organisation in a place so small, just putting up a team at all is probably the greatest achievement.
 Back-of-the-envelope maths puts the male population from 20-40 years old on the islands at around 500, meaning the pool of cricketers is incredibly shallow, and like many small ICC Members, those involved on the national board play several roles.
 Alexander on top of captaincy, runs the side as the coach, and acts as coach for the women's side and across junior programs on top of secretary roles for the Cricket Association.
 Though when the going gets tough, figures stand up.
 Step forward: Andy Brownlee.
 Not only the Vice Chair of the Falkland Islands National Sports Council, Brownlee turns out for the national cricket team, an exceptional effort considering he turned 64 years of age in October.
 Alexander paid tribute to his teammate, while shedding light on the difficulties of putting together a team.
 "He held the world record for the oldest debutant in a men’s T20I match, and he held the record for the oldest player as well until this week, when one of the Costa Rica players was 65 years old (Armando Foster) and took that title away from him.”
 "Most of the people currently in the team are expats who have moved here some time ago. Some St Helenians, some South Africans, others from the UK, one from Pakistan and one from Nepal.
 "There are a few locals that were born and grew up in the Falklands who would have played in this series but were not available.
 "It's difficult to put a good team together obviously because of the eligibility criteria, if they've not been here long enough, they don't qualify.
 "So we are always struggling. Last year we had a player that became eligible, but he didn't have his passport, the physical passport in his hand, so he couldn't fly (to Costa Rica)."
 As for the future, the building blocks are in place for more representation on the international stage, and on the women's side there too is progress.
 The group play intra-group matches and eight-a-side games in Stanley to help the group sharpen their skills, and there are plans to tour Saint Helena in January.
 “Our women's team is also quite a mixture, made up of a lot of teachers, mostly from the UK. 
 “(We have) quite a big, local, presence as well in our women's team.
 “We want to make the world know that the Falklands, we are doing our bit, we are trying our hardest and it is just that, if you put your mind to it, and you have the right group of people together that's determined to make something work, it definitely can happen. 
 “Even when we went to Costa Rica last year, not really knowing what to expect and where we are at, it was all about the small victories, having the opportunity to take your first wicket, scoring your first run, taking your first catch and just celebrating those small victories.
 “It's not always about the big end goal and the big prize, but there's a lot of journeys or positives that you can take along the way, while trying to reach that goal."
